title: Having More Left Me With Less
author: Wisdom From Dad
summary: In this Wisdom From Dad essay, the author traces his family's escalation from a $335-a-month one-bedroom apartment to a four-bedroom house with a pool, boats, jet skis, and a travel trailer, arguing that each acquisition quietly cost him something more valuable than money: time, freedom, and connection with his children. The turning point of the piece is his son's unprompted remark that he wished they had stayed in the smaller house because it was simpler, which the author uses to reframe 'bigger' as a hidden tax on attention and weekends rather than a straightforward upgrade in quality of life. Drawing on his own frugal, 94-year-old father, Greg McKeown's 90-percent rule from Essentialism, and Seneca on the misuse of time, he argues that every possession makes ongoing claims on capital, time, storage, and attention, so the real cost question is not affordability but whether an acquisition serves what actually matters. The piece closes with three questions the author now applies before any major purchase or commitment, reframing simplicity as a form of love and protection for family time rather than mere minimalism.
points: The essay's central reframe is that possessions impose ongoing, often invisible costs beyond price: capital, time, maintenance, storage, and attention, and it is these hidden costs, not the sticker price, that erode family time.

The son's remark, 'I wish we had stayed in the little house; it was so much simpler,' functions as the piece's turning point, converting an abstract simplicity argument into a concrete parenting regret.

The author uses the two-year swimming pool build, finished only after his daughter lost interest in it, as a specific illustration of how acquisition timelines can outlast the family need they were meant to serve.

He operationalizes McKeown's 'if it isn't at least a 90 percent yes, treat it as a no' rule and Seneca's warnings about wasted time into three concrete questions to ask before any purchase, renovation, or commitment.

The piece explicitly distinguishes its version of simplicity from minimalism, defining it instead as intentionality about what is allowed to make ongoing claims on a family's limited time and attention.
quotes: We didn't know it then, but that little water fight taught me something I've spent decades learning the hard way: bigger isn't always better.
What started by me asking the wrong question created a chain of events that cost us a lot of money, yes, but more than that, it cost me time, and freedom, and connection with what mattered most.
My son said it best. I don't remember how old he was, but he was not yet a teenager when he said, "I wish we had stayed in the little house; it was so much simpler.
Because everything you own asks something of you. It takes capital to buy it. Time and money to maintain it. Space to store it. Attention to manage it.

Ask these three questions: Is this aligned with what matters most? Does this move me toward the life I actually want, or simply give me more of something I think I want? Will it serve my family in the long run?
Because the goal isn't to build the biggest life you can afford. It's to build a life that gives you the time, freedom and energy to be the man your family needs you to be.
